newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-ELS FIGHTS BACK FROM SIX DOWN TO WIN AT LAST HOLE.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-ELS FIGHTS BACK FROM SIX DOWN TO WIN AT LAST HOLE.

text.p: Title-holder Ernie Els produced one of the finest comebacks in World Matchplay history on Friday when he fought back from six holes down after 18 to beat Steve Stricker at the last hole.
The big South African chipped in twice from off the green on the front nine of the afternoon round and rolled in a 33-footer to save par at the 27th as he closed the gap on the American.

Two down at that point, he finally drew level with a six-iron to four feet for birdie at the 33rd and won at the 501-yard par five last hole with a birdie as Stricker drove into a bunker and could only make par.
Els almost missed his final three-foot putt but it caught the side of the hole and fell in.

"To come back from six holes down -- it's kind of like a dream come true," the world number four said. "At the start of the second round I was just hoping to get to the last nine holes. It was very satisfying."
"Steve was all over me in the morning. I couldn't get started and I had no confidence," Els said. "I didn't think I had much of a chance this afternoon the way I played this morning."
The victory kept alive Els's bid to become the first player ever to win this title three times. He has now won seven matches without defeat since his debut in 1994.
It was the best comeback in this event since 1982 when Sandy Lyle recovered from six down to beat Nick Faldo.
The best-ever comeback was in 1965 -- the second time the tournament was staged -- when Els's compatriot Gary Player beat American Tony Lema at the 37th after being seven down after 19.
U.S. PGA champion Mark Brooks beat European number one Colin Montgomerie by one hole in a battle between the fourth and fifth seeds. Brooks faces Els in Saturday's semifinals.
The other two matches were one-sided.

Vijay Singh of Fiji upset third-seed U.S. Open champion Steve Jones nine and eight while second seed and British Open champion Tom Lehman crushed fellow American Mark O'Meara six and five. Singh and Lehman meet in the other semifinal.
The afternoon round between Els and Stricker was a reversal of the morning, when the 29-year-old American fired six birdies against only one from Els -- at the 18th.
After the break it was the South African's turn. He made eight birdies and two bogeys while Stricker could only birdie the short 28th hole.
But his first chip-in, from 25 feet at the 21st, was followed by a conceded birdie at the next, a nine-footer to win the 25th and another 25-foot chip-in at the 26th.
"I think that kind of got to Steve a little," said Els, who turned 27 on Thursday.
After a bogey at the 28th he was four under for the last eight holes while Stricker could not birdie any.
Brooks, a quiet 35-year-old Texan, had a see-saw battle with Montgomerie but moved in front with a 22-foot putt at the 33rd only to lose the next as Montgomerie drew level.
Then the American struck killer blows at the 571-yard 35th, hitting his third shot from the rough to eight feet from the pin and holing for a birdie.
Both men birdied the last, Brooks calmly holing from eight feet to secure victory.
"He holed out beautifully and he got up and down well," Montgomerie said afterwards.
"That's a fair analysis," Brooks agreed. "But I felt I played poor golf today, yet when you add the scores up it probably wasn't that bad."
Singh, who ousted fifth seed Phil Mickelson, used another strong start to take control against Jones.
"I made only two bogeys this morning and none this afternoon. If he was going to beat me he was going to have to do it with birdies," the Fijian said.
There have been only two quicker wins in the event -- Tom Watson's 11 and 9 over South African Dale Hayes in 1978 and Gary Player's 10 and 9 over Frenchman Jean Garaialde in 1969.
The powerful Lehman was too strong for O'Meara as he opened a three-hole lead on the morning front nine which he never looked likely to relinquish.
He seemed untroubled by playing in chilly, wet weather just days after playing in Phoenix, in the United States, in temperatures of 32 degrees celsius.
"It's nice to play in inclement weather," he said. "You get pretty sick of the heat living in the desert."
